utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We'll go into private session and the witness can be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I think you are aware that for the purposes of your own security I'll be referring to you as K89 for the duration of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And with the leave of the Court I'd like to start by showing you a document and that is 65 ter number 02578 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I just want you to look at it and tell me whether or not the information contained thereon reflect your personal details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it be shown to the Defence, please. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I think I should indicate that the 65 ter number is 02598.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You tender that under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01272 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K89, do you recall attending this Tribunal before, particularly on the 24th and the 25th of January, 2007, to give evidence in the trial of Mr. Milutinovic and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stamp kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since you have been here on this occasion, have you had an opportunity to review the transcript or record of your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is the evidence recorded in the transcript true and accurate to the best of your recollection and belief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is, if you were to be asked the same questions that you were asked -- if you were to be asked the same question that you were asked on that occasion, will your answers be the same or significantly substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the transcript -- the transcript, Your Honours, is 05115, and I tender it and ask that it be received as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01273 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there's a public redacted version of the said same transcript. It's 05353, which I also ask to be received as a normal exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01274.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness in his previous testimony at pages 9154 to 956 -- that is 9154 to 9156 of the transcript had marked two maps to refer to places that his evidence related to. May I just inquire of the Court whether it would be preferable to have him remark those marks or else I could tender those two maps that he marked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. The maps are 05116 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite sure whether I understood Mr. Stamp correctly. Is he proposing these two documents to be tendered into evidence? I apologise if I am upon my feet without reason, but the proposal would be by the Defence that those two maps are not going to take up too much time before this Trial Chamber, that they be marked again because I think the Defence will be using it during its examination. So that would be useful if we were to do that now and not to admit maps which have already been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They, by order of the Court, have now already been received in evidence. I am afraid your cross-examination may have to go over territory again. Carry on please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the record they are 05116 and 05117. And they were referred to in the transcript as IC115 and IC116 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the Registrar is about to give them the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, should the document be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's any need for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 05116 will be Exhibit P01275, and 65 ter 05117 will be Exhibit P01276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K89, I just have one or two questions by way of clarification in respect to your previous testimony which we have on record and it's pretty comprehensive. You said when you were last here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, that is page 9127 of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that during the period from the 25th of March and for about 20 to 23 days thereafter your unit was involved in participating in search activities in the vicinity between Orahovac and Djakovica; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I ask that question, I just recall that it has been the practice of the Court for a short summary to be read. I don't know if it's necessary in this case. I could proceed to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be helpful and you might also confirm whether you meant page 9127?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the particular point I was coming to in the questioning is at that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Summary please, and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The witness is a former member of the Army of Yugoslavia who was deployed in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. And the witness in his testimony described the uniforms and the weapons that he was issued with and the training that he received prior to his deployment in Kosovo. In 1998, the witness's unit was deployed to a VJ camp in Sulani near Djakovica where mortars and artillery were set up and they fired on several targets from that position, particularly upon the village of Smolnica or towards the direction of the village of Smolnica. The witness remained -- the witness and the unit remained in that area for about three to four months, and he testified that on at least one occasion in August 1998 his unit was instructed to fire at the Smolnica mosque where they were told that there were KLA persons present. Around September or October 1998 the witness's unit moved from Sulani to Zub, and from that position the witness's unit continued to fire towards the area of the town of Smolnica. And at that position the witness's unit remained, that is Zup, until the beginning of hostilities on the 24th of March, 1999. On that day, the -- some members of the witness's unit were deployed for operations in the villages between Djakovica and Orahovac. Just before they set off for those operations, their commander or a senior commander in the VJ told them that not a single Albanian ear [Realtime transcript read in error "heir"] was to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn so as to prevent them from coming back. The witness and his units took part in house-to-house searches in the area for 20 to 23 days where they searched for weapons and KLA personnel. He describes that there were different groups involved together or different arms group -- armed groups operating together with the VJ in these search operations including the police and also members of Arkan's Tigers. And he describes the uniforms and other paraphernalia worn by the different groups. On one occasion during these search operations, the witness saw members of the VJ separate about 15 to 20 men from the women and children that were members of a refugee convoy and executing these men by shooting them. He testified that these victims were ordered to don KLA uniforms prior to being shot. His evidence also described in general the torching of the houses on orders that they received from their superiors and on the presence of large convoys of women and children of Albanian -- Kosovo Albanian women, children, men, and other civilians who had left their homes and were heading for the Albanian border. And he also testified that these convoys were stopped many times on the road and their identity documents were taken away and torn up by members of the armed forces. The witness also testified that he assisted in loading bodies, approximately 8 of them who had been shot and who were dressed in civilian clothes and being ordered to escort them by lorry to the power-station near Pristina called Obilic where the bodies were left with other members of the VJ. These bodies were collected from villages in the area of Orahovac. Thank you very much, Your Honour, that is a summary of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K89, if I may get back to the question I was asking you earlier, you said at 9127 of the transcript that during these operations that you were involved in at the villages near to Orahovac, among the armed forces that were involved in the searches of the people were policemen and Arkan's Tigers and you said that you did not know who commanded the Tigers, Arkan's Tigers. Can you tell us on how many occasions you saw members or persons who were described to you or appeared to be Arkan's Tigers participating in search operations with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I might have seen them twice perhaps. I can't remember exactly. A little before the attack started. And then afterwards around Orahovac. It was September, March, April -- no, April, I think, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When they were operating in the field with the police involved in these searches, can you say how they travelled, by what means they travelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know by what means. I saw them going on foot. They were walking as a unit, and infantry. Perhaps they had their vehicle, I'm sure they did, some military vehicle, but we thought -- we said to each other, Who are these different uniforms? And then they said, Well they're Arkan's Tigers. But we didn't have any contacts with them at all. I didn't know they were those men. We had no contacts. I was just told they were Arkan's Tigers, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when they were involved in these searches, about how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how many. There were quite a few of them. I don't know. There were soldiers and policemen and the others. I don't know how many there were exactly, I can't remember. I can't give you a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these persons that were described as the Arkan's Tigers, for about how long did you see them present participating in the search operation with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. At the beginning -- well, two or three days when we were there, they were already there and then we stayed on last because we were provided security for our soldiers, our infantry as a sort of protection, as a shield, and we didn't see them any more after that. So I don't know how long they were there, were they there for one day or more, I don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first time you came across those persons that you referred to as Arkan's Tigers while you were in Kosovo, was when? Can you remember approximately when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the date was, but I don't think the NATO forces -- well, there wasn't any NATO bombing when they were passing by. Now, where they were going -- well, we had some water -- we didn't have any water at Zub where we were, but we had to go down there. Perhaps they had a tent there or something. I really don't know, I don't know how they came to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where was it that you encountered them first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was below Zub. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to something else. You also spoke about the killing of some 15 to 20 men who were taken from a column, forced to don KLA uniforms, and then shot execution style by members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is at 9137 and 9144 of the transcripts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also said that you saw someone that you call (redacted) do it. Just to be clear about your testimony, there are just one or two things that I'm not entirely clear. I'd like to just go over with you what exactly you saw. Did you see when VJ soldiers separate -- or may I just withdraw that and put it this way: Did you see how the men were separated from the women in the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see them being taken away to the place where they were shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where is it they were when they were forced to change their civilian clothes into KLA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were about a hundred metres away from us roughly. They were to the left of us. It was the surrounding area of Orahovac. I don't know which village exactly. They have a different accent, so I can't say which village they came from. But I know that it was in the surrounding area of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I just want us to focus just for a couple of minutes on the incident itself, not generally where they are from. Did you see the person or the persons who fired on them and killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We were there, the column of refugees came by, and some people were freed there or released. These were individuals. I don't know if they were in the KLA army or what, but they were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but just please try to just focus on what I'm asking you now. The firing of the machine-gun on to the men, the 15 or 20 men who had been taken apart, did you see that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said it was (redacted) who fired with a machine-gun, can you explain why you said it was (redacted) who fired with the machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true that I said that it was (redacted), but in my opinion he was using a machine-gun. And any soldier issued with a weapon and handling one, I mean, I don't know. I cannot -- I said that then, but now I'm not sure. It's possible, everyone was wearing the same uniforms, it's possible it was somebody else. Perhaps regular soldiers should not behave like that. I'm not sure, I cannot be sure. I don't know. I mean, there was fire from the machine-gun. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who -- which soldier, which member of your unit normally had possession of the machine-gun that was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from our unit because we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I remember correctly, the witness did not mention that (redacted) was from his unit, so I don't know what the reference would be to put the question in this particular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Just checking that ... I don't see any particular reference to the unit, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I could just save time by doing it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who normally had possession of the machine-gun that was used to do the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The infantry had machine-guns, light machine-guns. (redacted) was using one. Other than him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you saw the soldier fire on the group of men, could you see that soldier's face from the distance you were at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't see because he had his back to me, so I wasn't able to see. Even if he had been facing me, I wouldn't have been able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, at the place where the men were separated from the women and the event occurred, apart from the VJ, were there other armed forces in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you remember the approximate date of this event? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime in April, the 7th or the 8th, but I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, K89. Your Honours, I have nothing further for the witness for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Is it you, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. K89. I'm Aleksandar Popovic in the Defence team of Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, and I'm here with Ms. Marie O'Leary and Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic. I'm going to put some questions to you in reference to your statement. But I would like to ask you, since we speak the same language, please to wait for me to complete my question and to reply after that so that we can make it possible for the interpreters to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, I'm so sorry to interrupt. Your Honours, I had intended, and I am afraid it's not a very good morning for me. When we were mentioning a particular name of one of the members of his unit, I had intended to ask to go into private session for that, and somehow something happened and I completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we redact the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely agree with Mr. Stamp, but I would like to repeat one more time that that was not a member of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. K89, would I be correct if I were to say that you provided two statements to date: the first one to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal on the 23rd of January, 2006; and the second one in the Milutinovic et al. case on the 24th and 25th of January, 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to look at your statement from January 2006. Did you have the opportunity, after providing the statement, to read it back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity in that statement to make any corrections of anything that was not a reflection of what you had actually said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were some things -- well, I cannot remember everything, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And that statement of the 26th of January, 2006, reflect faithfully the events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me when you went to serve your military term of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on the 18th of March, 1998. I went to Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you go to serve your military term of duty? Did you receive a regular summons and after that report to the mobilisation office, or was it in some other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to report voluntarily to join the army, just like all the citizens go, and then I received a summons from -- and then I was sent to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you voluntarily applied to go and serve your military term of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of the statement from January 2006 you say: "In February of 1998 I received papers or a summons to serve the regular military term of duty in the Army of Yugoslavia." So did you receive a summons which would be the usual procedure, or did you, as you have just said, report voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, I went that month and asked the officials in the recruitment office to send me. I went there voluntarily and then I was sent a summons to report there in March 1998, to report to such and such a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say it was like this, that you went that month, which month are you talking about in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was February 1998, perhaps late February, to receive a pre-summons, then you get some money for the trip, and then I received the actual summons on the 13th or the 14th of March, the proper summons to which barracks to report and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, can we be precise now, what summons are you talking about when you refer in your statement that you received a papers ordering me to serve that national service in February 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to understand it correctly, you receive a pre-summons, I think that was in February. This was the pre-summons. And then the actual summons with the stamp and the money is something that you receive in March. This was a couple of days before the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So after receiving the summons, you were sent to the Valjevo barracks. Am I correct when I say that you went through basic infantry training in the Valjevo barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that your military specialty or the VES was the infantry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the basic infantry training that you went through in Valjevo takes two months and 23 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And you went through this whole training in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if I was there for the entire duration, but we were there for two months, two months and a bit in Valjevo. Then it was a little bit accelerated, so I don't know. But we probably were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that during the basic infantry training that you completed in Valjevo there is a part that is conducted in classrooms of a closed type and which is conducted in the form of lectures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that in the course of the theoretical part of the training, there is a part that refers to the conduct of soldiers in peacetime and wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there is, but, well, perhaps I wasn't there when that was being taught but probably there is something about conduct, but I did not really learn that. I learned the insignia, the signage, about the rifles. I mean, but it should be there, the rules for the conduct of a soldier, but I didn't learn that. I don't know for what reason why, but it definitely should be part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct when I say that members of the infantry, after the basic infantry training, are transferred and deployed in accordance with the requirements of the army to the appropriate locations and assigned to the tasks that are required?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say that after you completed the basic training as an infantry man were sent from Valjevo to Djakovica? I think you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that you actually completed the entire infantry training period, and that after that you were sent on for your further duties where you would go through further training in the course of serving your military term of duty in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether we passed the regular training or accelerated training, I have no idea, but I think we did complete it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when you arrived in Djakovica, what date that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the date was, whether it was the end of May or beginning of June. I really can't remember. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. K89, when you arrived at the barracks in Djakovica, which unit were you assigned to? Which brigade, battalion, company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at the barracks and from there, well, we stayed there for an hour or two, and then we were sent off to a mountain post at Zub. And I was in the 120th Mortar Company. I think it belongs to the infantry, that one, I'm not quite sure. But I think I was assigned to the infantry generally speaking with a mortar of 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: K89, have I understood you correctly. Did you say that you belonged to the company that was 120 millimetres, but do you remember the brigade or battalion you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you left the barracks in Djakovica? And we are still talking about 1998 after your arrival from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't even spend the night in the barracks. We were just there on the day we arrived. And from Pristina to Djakovica, it might have been the afternoon or later, anyway, we were there -- in Djakovica for two or three hours where we were issued rifles, helmets, another set of uniforms, and were driven in trucks up to our positions. Because before that, up at those positions there was a previous unit, and they had just completed their military service, that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Sulani, I think, whether that's the village - or is it a mountain? - because -- it's probably the village. It's called Sulani. But there was a mountain above the village, but I think it was -- Sulani was the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have a look at 65 ter 0065. It's a map. And page 21 of that, please. It's a 65 ter exhibit. 615. I think that's page 27. We need page 21. Thank you. That's it. May we zoom in, please. That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, K89, do you see on that map some of the villages that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all I can see here is Zub. Whether it's a village or a mountain, I don't know, but that's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you try and find this village Sulani that you referred to on the map. Since you found the other place, perhaps that will give you a better orientation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't find Sulani. But I do see Zoi [as interpreted] it's somewhere -- well, as I said, is that the name of a mountain or is it the name of something else, I'm not sure. And I can't find Sulani on this map, which is where our position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I haven't managed to find it either. I can't see Sulani. But as you know, the surrounding places you were in - and since you know, as you've already told us, and we'll get back to that later on - what places were targets, can you use that to find your way around this map and show us roughly where this place Sulani might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it should be somewhere around Zub and northwards, we were in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a marker and mark in this area where you think you were. Draw it in on the map and put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think it's somewhere here. But as I say, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you place the number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the distance was from this place that you've marked to Smolnica? If you can see Smolnica on the map, can you put a 2 next to Smolnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You haven't told me yet what the distance was from Sulani to Smolnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the distance was exactly. It was across the hill. As the crow flies, perhaps 5 or 6 kilometres. But I'm not quite sure. I don't know the exact distance from Sulani to Smolnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and refresh your memory. Now, in paragraph 15 of your statement of January 2006, the last sentence there when you're referring to which villages you targeted from Sulani, you say: "The village was called Smolnica and was 8 or 9 kilometres north of our position."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. As I say again, I'm not quite sure what the exact distance was. It might have been even more than 9 kilometres. I'm not a hundred per cent certain how many kilometres there are from Sulani to Smolnica because it's across the hill. It's over the hill, so I couldn't really calculate the distance or see it. But judging by the mortars, it might have been 7 or 8 kilometres, maybe closer, maybe further.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The distance we are referring to is the distance you mention in the Milutinovic trial. Now, am I right in saying that in any event you remember the distance better in 2006 when you spoke about it than you are today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, mostly the same, 2006 just like today. As I say, I'm not quite sure. Now, whether -- even 2006 was seven or eight years later, so I can't remember what the exact distance was and what the exact village was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: K89, from the time you arrived in Sulani, you were one of the servers, one of the crew on a 120 millimetre mortar; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Sulani. But staying with this map for just a moment, after Sulani, you went to Zub; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we mark Zub on the map, let me ask you this: Do you know what the range of a 120 millimetre mortar is and can you explain to us whether this depends on the filling or something else? On the charge or on something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact range of the mortar. I think there are some special mines that are used, or some special charges, but I don't really know what its exact range is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that the range with a 600 [as interpreted] charge, and is a 600 charge the highest charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think there is an error in the transcript, it says 600. I said 6, a 6th charge. Would you agree with me that the range of a 120 millimetre mortar with a 6th charge is 6.300 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does not range vary with altitude and temperature?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maximum range with a 6th charge judging by the literature and this information of commanders of mortar units is 6.300 metre, and that's what I base my question on. Yes, it can vary, but I think we are talking about a maximum range here, that that figure is the maximum range.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, witness would you agree with me that the maximum range of a 120 millimetre mortar with a 5th charge is 5.500 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When we are on the subject, let me ask you this, do you consider a reliable source information from the commander who was -- is a captain now, (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do agree with him, (redacted). I suppose he knows about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: K89, I'm asking you this for the simple reason that you said that from Sulani - and you marked Sulani - that you targeted Smolnica. Now, in your statements - and I quoted paragraph 15, and you repeated this in the Milutinovic trial. It says that Smolnica was 8 or 9 kilometres away from Sulani. Now, if we take into account the range that I mentioned for the 120 millimetre mortar, can you explain to us how it was possible to target Smolnica from Sulani then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I said that we targeted in that direction, in the direction of Smolnica. I don't know whether we could have hit Smolnica or not. I couldn't see it. It's not flat land, it's across the hill. So I wasn't clear on what we were targeting. Perhaps there was another village in front of Smolnica. I don't know what Smolnica is in fact - is it a village or a town? - perhaps the KLA had a stronghold, perhaps the Albanians had a stronghold around the village or in the village itself, but I'm not quite clear on that. I don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude that you actually don't know if you could hit Smolnica from Sulani with mortar fire? When I say Smolnica, I think of the village of Smolnica. But you just had the information to fire in the direction of Smolnica wherever that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So to continue with Sulani, when you came to Sulani --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could move to a private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, because I interrupt you. Our client again didn't receive the translation and at the first session there was no any translation for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can only be to do with some switch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will speak now to see whether a translation comes through to your client. No, still nothing. I will try once again to see whether something comes. It appears the answer is no translation is reaching. Are we on the correct channel? Perhaps try the other channels to see whether the translation comes through. I will keep speaking here in the hope that we can find a channel. I wonder whether any of the arrangements now have produced sound for the accused? If I remember the last time this occurred, it was merely a matter of a switch not having been thrown. I will speak again. Yes, well it certainly is coming through on the Judges' sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are the earphones working on other channels? I think the channel should be channel 6 that is selected. Can we now have some translation to test again. The problem is overcome. Thank you. And thank you for the interpreters who kept talking with me. Could I suggest that if your client has any problem in future, he should indicate straightaway so that there is no continuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There will be no more further problems about that because we already make a deal about that that he intervene immediately if he have any problem with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking about crossing from Sulani into Zub. Can you tell us whether the whole unit crossed over to Zub, or was the situation different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole unit crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you then, in view of your answer, of paragraph 23 of your statement. In the first sentence you say: "Only two of the mortars from our company went to Zub." Now, which is it, what you said in your statement or is the truth what you are telling us here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: From Sulani, we withdrew on the 24th of March when the bombing started because two of the mortar men went to Zub, and we went to the environs of Orahovac, some 20 of us, or whatever, we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a little confusing and quite different from what you said earlier. Let's take it step by step. When did you move from Sulani to Zub?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how it was: On the 24th of March, it might have been the 25th. We went from Sulani, most of us, the majority of us, with two mortars, we went to -- around the village of Orahovac, and the unit was withdrawing from Zub. And what remained of our mortar unit, they transferred to Zub. And that was after the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the 24th of March, 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How, then, are we to understand what you said in paragraph 22 of your statement and in the Milutinovic transcript where you say: "Around September or October 1998, we moved from Sulani to Zub"? So my question to you is this: Did you move from Sulani to Zub in September or October 1998 or the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly, we changed around. Moved our positions. So maybe it was -- well, whether it was 1998 or 1999, we moved our positions, we went round from Sulani to Zub, to an outpost that was called Deva. Now, when this was, when we changed our positions, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that you don't actually know when you moved from Sulani to Zub?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been straightaway, but I really can't remember. I'm not sure. Whether it was before NATO or after NATO, 1998 or 1999. I really can't say. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try and summarise everything you've said so far. Can you be as precise as possible. Where were you personally from the moment you arrived in Sulani which was June 1998, up until the beginning of the NATO bombing, that is to say the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, mostly we were at Zub, at Sulani, underneath the Deva outpost, those were our positions. Now, where we were exactly when the NATO bombing started, whether we were at Zub or Sulani, I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just not clear on one point. Were you at Zub or not at Zub before the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 24th of March, 1999, do you remember what happened then on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what your movements were on that day? Where were you? Was there any interesting event that happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know where we were going. We didn't move around a lot because NATO started its bombing. So whether that was early in the morning of the 25th or not. Anyway, one unit went there, went to Orahovac or the vicinity of Orahovac, and where our positions were exactly, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, might your unit have been moving towards Deva on the 24th to replace another unit that was up there. And I'm quoting from part of your statement, so I just want to know whether you stand by what you said then or do you have something different to tell us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just indicate what part of the statement, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. It's paragraph 25 which says: "On the 24th of March, we were moving to relieve one of the units in Deva." The first sentence of paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how they understood it. I didn't go. Well, our unit didn't to relieve anyone, but to protect this outpost Deva, so that the NATO forces, well, or the infantry was coming from Albania, and the KLA. So we defended this border post or Deva outpost.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you set out from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean from what place?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether we were at Zub or Sulani at that point in time. Anyway, we were moving towards the Deva border post. I know when we were withdrawing from Orahovac that we were underneath the Deva outpost. Whether it was to the left or the right of Deva, and the Babaj Boks border post. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if I heard you correctly, you said something that wasn't recorded. You said you yourself didn't go to Deva; is that right? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did go, but after the 24th, some 20 days after the 24th, when we were around Orahovac village and were withdrawing we were up at the positions there. So I was there afterwards. But I didn't go there straightaway. I didn't go there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let us conclude. On the 24th, you did not go to Deva but you went towards Deva on -- the first time 20 days later when you returned to Orahovac; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 25 you state in the first sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before I read this, I would just like to ask the Chamber if we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, now I'm going to move to the part when your unit was sent to Orahovac. Can you please tell me what the primary task of your unit was when you were sent to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think our task -- I don't think, I know that our task was to follow the infantry who were going in front of us and that we were supposed to look out and guard their back in case anyone from the villages opened fire so that we would then be able to fire at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So am I correct in saying that you were practically the rear unit that was supposed to provide fire support to the infantry units on the frontline, support with your 120 millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me how far the rear unit should be behind the first line of infantry in order to be able to provide fire support to them, the 120 millimetre unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I think at least half a kilometre back. I don't know precisely what the distance should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept if I were to say that the distance between the rear 120 millimetre mortar unit that is supposed to provide fire support to the first line of infantry should be at least 1.500 metres? Again I'm talking about someone who was the commander of your company and also the fact that I consulted some military manuals, those are the sources for my assertion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to provide this fire support properly, did you also need to have a firing position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to have a proper firing position, a constructed fire position in order to be able to provide fire support? I'm talking about a posted observer at a certain distance who would be reporting of the direction and the range required in order to achieve precise fire, and that the mortars would need to be placed at an elevation or in a valley in order to achieve the required results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that should have been like that. Probably my observer or spotter was somewhere. I don't know. I mean, we were just part of the infantry. We didn't actually set up the mortars. They were on the back of the truck. We didn't take them down and install them anywhere. We didn't have a specific position.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this specific case when you were firing in the environs of Orahovac, how far away from you from the first infantry lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not use any mortars in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I wasn't asking you if you used them. I assume that the fact whether you would use them or not didn't depend on you or not but on whether the infantry needed mortar fire or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: You, as the firing support for infantry units, how far back were you from the first infantry lines when you were in the environs of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we might have been 150 to 200 metres behind them, or perhaps closer. I'm not quite sure. We weren't too far off.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So from a distance of 150 to 200 metres, you were supposed to give fire-power support to the 120 millimetre mortars at their positions; right? Is that at all possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's the distance we were at. Perhaps they knew no support would be needed. I don't know why we were at that distance if we weren't able to provide fire support from where we were at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you help me with something. You've told us that the mortars, you didn't unload from the trucks. They remained on the trucks, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct, they were attached to the trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: K89, if you were at a distance of 150 to 200 metres from the infantry frontline, am right in saying that you and your mortars were under threat, were jeopardized by the fire-power of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you change your testimony if I were to tell you that Lieutenant (redacted), whom we've already mentioned, gave a statement to the Tribunal's investigators and that in that statement he said that you never approach closer to 1 kilometre from the frontline, infantry frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. Perhaps what he said was true, but I know that we were there in that area, and that we were at that distance. Now, why we were at that distance, I'm not quite clear. But we did go together with them. We also went on our own. We were there for a couple of days, just our mortar unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: There's a difference in what he says and what you say. In fact, it's the exact opposite. There's an enormous amount of difference. If you say that what he says might be true, then some of what you said or what he said -- well, the truth can't be both ways, so would you change your testimony if I put it to you that that is what he said? Do you allow for the possibility of him being right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's asked and answered and most of his question is composed of arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can certainly clarify whether the witness holds to his position that at least at times he was just 150 to 200 metres or something like that behind the frontline. If he holds to that, I don't think you need anything more, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was just prompted by what the witness said when he said that perhaps what (redacted) is saying was correct, was the truth. That's the only reason I went on to ask him my subsequent question, but we can move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying you can ask him whether he remains his view that they were at times only 150 to 200 metres behind. You have already told him what the lieutenant said.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to paragraph 28 of your statement dated January 2006 and the events you talked about in the Milutinovic trial. Here you refer to the event when you actually saw the killing. And my question to you linked to this paragraph is this: Was it a terrible event that imprinted itself on your mind and do you remember it so well that you can provide us with more detailed information linked to this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the army. Of course, I didn't like seeing what was happening. I didn't take it lightly. Well, I don't know. I saw what I saw and it did embed itself in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now my first question is, do you remember where this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the environs of Orahovac. I don't remember which village exactly, or the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your 2006 statement when you refer to this event, you say that, just let me find that passage: "If they were wearing civilian clothes they would dress them in KLA uniforms." Now, my first question linked to that is this: Does that mean that among them there were some people who did not have civilian clothes on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and explain. It says here, "if they were wearing civilian clothes." When you say "if they were wearing," I'm asking you whether it was possible that they were wearing something else? Wearing other clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they just had civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So all of them were wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say -- you go on to say: "... they would dress them in KLA uniforms." Can you tell us how you saw these -- what those uniforms looked like? Can you tell us what the uniforms looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the uniforms were similar -- well, the colour was lighter. It was rather like the Yugoslav Army uniforms but with different insignias on the shoulders. They had the UCK or KLA insignia. They were similar to the Yugoslav Army uniforms, but the colour was different. It wasn't the same shade. But not much different.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you are speaking about uniforms, you talk about pants, jackets, what do you mean when you say "uniform"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, trousers, jackets, just like any uniform. Just like the Yugoslav Army uniforms. But theirs was a bit different; it wasn't like ours. There were some red ones. Well, there was more colour on their uniforms than the Yugoslav Army ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened, can you describe what happened? They ordered what? They ordered the civilians to take their uniforms off and put on the other ones or what? Can you explain what they actually did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a column, they were refugees, mostly men but women too. And they separated some of them, a couple of them. There might have been some younger people too, whether they had received information saying that these people had been in the army or whatever, that, I don't know, but I saw them changing clothes and putting uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with that for a moment. When you say "I saw them putting uniforms on them," can you tell us what it was they ordered and what items of clothing they were putting on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they were ordered to do. Probably they were told to take off their civilian clothes and put on the uniforms because they were 1-, or 200 metres away from us, so I couldn't hear what they were actually saying. I couldn't hear any order being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And what parts of the uniform were they putting on? What items of clothing, of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. As I say, their uniforms were similar to ours. Probably it was the uniform of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what parts of uniforms these civilians were putting on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the entire uniform set; trousers, shirts, jackets. The lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 28 of your statement of January 2006, you also say the following: "I saw one man making a video recording of how the soldiers were dressing the bodies of the UCK -- of the bodies in UCK uniforms." Am I right saying that you are talking about dead people and not living people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said they were -- no, they were putting on the uniforms themselves. They weren't dead bodies. The people themselves, the civilians, they were putting on these uniforms. So possibly there was a misunderstanding, perhaps they didn't understand what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: But you are talking about a man video recording this, filming it, filming the soldiers dressing the bodies in KLA uniforms. There's no mention here of anybody taking off their clothes and putting on uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did see a man. I and another person were there. Whether he had a camera or whether he was making a recording of some kind, he had something in his hand anyway, and he ran away when he noticed us, the two of us. But let me say again -- well, perhaps I said that, but I don't think I said bodies. They were ordering them. I didn't hear the order. But anyway, they were putting on uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure whether they were putting on uniforms or maybe they were bodies that were being dressed in uniforms afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm certain that these people were putting on the uniforms themselves. That they weren't bodies. You mean dead bodies? They weren't dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just reading your words from the statement here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were living people.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you said that this person was recording something or filming something, what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was wearing civilian clothes. I don't really know. He wasn't very tall or anything. He was -- had brown hair. But you could see that he had something in his hands, that he was holding something. Whether it was a camera or whatever. I'm not sure. But he was standing behind -- the person next to me said he was probably filming this or recording this or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, just a few more questions in order -- that we have left to go through. First of all, one about Arkan's Tigers. Am I correct that the unit that you described as being a unit of Arkan's Tigers is something that you are not sure about, you don't know that personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yeah, it's true, I don't know that it was them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say that what you heard from someone does not mean that it is true? You allow for the possibility that that other person could have made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that you didn't see any markings or insignia which would indicate that the unit was what you said it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have any markings indicating Arkan's Tigers. They had these red or blue berets. They didn't have the coveralls that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct when I say that you didn't see their commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this something that should be in private? It could be a basis for identification. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was thanking you for your further attendance here and for the assistance that you have given. We have your evidence today and what you have said in your previous testimony which we will consider in due course. So you are now free to go back to your normal activities, and a Court Officer will assist you when we rise. We now adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th of August, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
